meta.blurb: A clerk, a secret shorthand and nine years of London life. Samuel Pepys wrote down his dinners, quarrels and music, then the plague, the Dutch war and the Great Fire. His honest voice still makes the seventeenth century feel close.
meta.bible: The Diary of Samuel Pepys: kept in shorthand from 1 January 1660 to 31 May 1669; six volumes now at Magdalene College, Cambridge. Samuel Pepys: born in London in 1633, son of a tailor; Clerk of the Acts at the Navy Office; later Secretary to the Admiralty and President of the Royal Society; died in 1703. Elizabeth Pepys: his wife, married in 1655 when she was fifteen; died in November 1669 aged twenty-nine. Edward Montagu: Pepys's cousin and patron, a powerful sea commander. Charles II: king restored in 1660, landed at Dover on 25 May. Duke of York: the King's brother, head of the Navy. General Monck: the general who helped bring back the king. Naseby: warship renamed the Royal Charles. Sir William Penn: Pepys's neighbour and Navy colleague. Sir Thomas Bloodworth: Lord Mayor during the Great Fire. Jane: Pepys's maid who woke him on 2 September 1666. Mr Pembleton: Elizabeth's dancing master. Deb Willet: Elizabeth's young companion. Robert Hooke: author of Micrographia. Christopher Wren and John Evelyn: men who planned a new London. John Smith: student who deciphered the shorthand. Places: London, Westminster, Axe Yard, Seething Lane, the Navy Office, the Tower of London, London Bridge, Whitehall, Drury Lane, Cannon Street, Deptford, the Medway, Lowestoft, Cambridge, St Olave's church in Hart Street, All Hallows Barking, Holland, the Netherlands, France. Events: the Rump Parliament, the Restoration and coronation of Charles II, the Great Plague of 1665, the Second Dutch War, the Four Days' Battle in 1666, the Great Fire of 2 to 6 September 1666, the Dutch raid on the Medway in June 1667. Voice and tone: warm, curious and honest, with gentle humour; real events kept accurate; dark episodes (plague, fire) treated factually and without gore; Pepys's faults are admitted plainly and politely.

B1B2: On the first day of 1660, a young London clerk named Samuel Pepys begins a diary. He writes in a secret kind of shorthand, because he plans to tell the whole truth about his life.
Samuel Pepys was born in London in 1633, the son of a tailor. He studied at Cambridge, but in 1660 he is still a poor clerk with little money and large hopes.
Two years earlier, Pepys had survived a dangerous operation to remove a stone from his bladder. Every year after that, on the same date in March, he gave a dinner to celebrate being alive.
Pepys is married to Elizabeth, whom he wed in 1655 when she was only fifteen. They love each other and they quarrel, and the diary records both with equal honesty.
In February 1660, Londoners light bonfires in every street to cheer General Monck and his army. They roast rumps of meat over the flames, to mock the weak Parliament known as the Rump.
In March 1660, Pepys joins his cousin, the sea commander Edward Montagu, aboard the warship Naseby. Soon the fleet will cross to Holland to bring the exiled Charles Stuart home to England.
On 25 May 1660, King Charles II steps ashore at Dover, and crowds cheer him all the way to London. The Naseby, Pepys's ship, is given a new name, the Royal Charles.
Thanks to his cousin, Pepys is made Clerk of the Acts at the Navy Office in 1660. The job brings a good salary and a house in Seething Lane, close to the Tower of London.
Pepys works long hours at the Navy Office, checking ships, stores and money. In 1662, aged twenty-nine, he even sets out to learn the multiplication table, because he wants to do his job properly.
On 23 April 1661, Pepys joins the crowds to see the coronation of King Charles II. In the evening he drinks far too much wine and goes to bed drunk, and he honestly writes it all down.

Pepys loves music above almost everything else, and he plays the violin, the lute and a small flute called the flageolet. Evenings at home are often spent in singing and playing with Elizabeth and their friends.
Pepys goes to the theatre again and again, and he writes honest opinions of every play. When he sees A Midsummer Night's Dream, he calls it the most dull and ridiculous play he has ever seen.
Pepys writes about his dinners in loving detail, from oysters and pies to roast meat and wine. He enjoys inviting friends to his table, and he is always proud when a meal goes well.
Pepys loves the new coffee-houses, where men gather to read the news, argue and make useful friends. In the diary they appear as lively places full of smoke, talk and gossip.
In 1663 Pepys decides to buy a wig, which is the latest fashion for gentlemen. He feels nervous, because he worries about the cost and about what people will say when they see it.
Pepys is honest about his faults, and he makes solemn promises to give up wine, plays and wasting time. He often keeps them for a few weeks, then breaks them, and he cheerfully writes that down too.
Elizabeth takes dancing lessons from a teacher named Mr Pembleton, and Pepys becomes very jealous. He watches them closely, and for days he cannot think about anything else.
In December 1664, a great comet appears in the sky, and Pepys goes out into the cold to see it. Many people are afraid of it, and they wonder what terrible thing will happen next.
In January 1665, Pepys buys Robert Hooke's Micrographia, a book full of drawings made with a microscope. He reads it until two in the morning and calls it the most ingenious book he has ever read.
In 1665 England goes to war against the Dutch, and Pepys works from morning until night to supply the ships. In June the English win a great battle off Lowestoft, and London celebrates.

On 7 June 1665, Pepys sees houses marked with a red cross for the first time in his life. The words “Lord have mercy upon us” are written on the door, and he feels so unwell that he buys tobacco to chew.
As the plague grows stronger, Pepys writes his will and arranges his money and papers. He sends Elizabeth and the household to a safer place down the river, but he stays at work in London.
In the late summer of 1665, Pepys walks through streets that are almost empty. Shops are shut, grass grows in the middle of Whitehall, and funeral bells ring all day long.
Friends, neighbours and workmen fall sick and die, and Pepys hears of new deaths every day. Even so, he goes on working at the Navy Office, because the ships still need food, sails and men.
In September 1665, the printed bill shows more than seven thousand deaths in one week. Pepys believes that the real number is nearer ten thousand, because the poor cannot all be counted.

By the end of 1665, the numbers of the dead have fallen, and Pepys sees more people in the streets. Shops reopen, and neighbours who avoided one another for months greet each other again with cautious smiles.

In June 1666, the sound of guns from a great sea battle is heard in the south-east of England. Pepys waits anxiously for news, and when it comes he learns that the English fleet has suffered heavy losses.
The government is running out of money, and the sailors are paid late or not at all. Pepys worries that angry men will leave the ships, and he pleads for more money.
In the dark hours of 2 September 1666, Pepys's maid Jane wakes him to report a big fire in the City. He looks from the window, decides that it is far enough away and goes back to bed.
In the morning Pepys hears that more than three hundred houses have already burned in the night. He climbs a high place in the Tower of London and sees the fire spreading along London Bridge.
Pepys takes a boat along the river and watches terrified people carrying their goods to safety. He notices pigeons that hover around their windows until their wings catch fire and they fall.
Pepys hurries to Whitehall and tells King Charles II and the Duke of York how badly the fire is spreading. The King orders that houses be pulled down to stop it, and soldiers are sent to help.

Pepys finds the Lord Mayor, Sir Thomas Bloodworth, in the street, so tired that he seems close to tears. He says that the people will not obey him and that the fire moves faster than his men can pull down houses.
That night, Pepys goes with friends to the south bank and sits in an alehouse to watch the fire. The flames form a great arch across the river, and the sky glows red like a furnace.
On Monday, Pepys packs his money, papers and goods and tries to find carts to carry them away. Carts are so rare that people pay huge sums, and the streets are crowded with frightened families.
On 4 September, Pepys and his neighbour, Sir William Penn, dig a pit in the garden. They bury their best wine and a wheel of Parmesan cheese, hoping that the earth will protect them from the fire.
Sir William Penn brings workmen from Deptford to pull down houses near the Navy Office. At the same time the wind drops, and the fire stops close to Pepys's home.
When the fire is finally over, Pepys walks through the ruins of the City. The ground is still so hot that it almost burns the soles of his shoes.

The Great Fire burned for about four days and destroyed some 13,000 houses and 87 churches, including old St Paul's. Tens of thousands of people lost their homes, although only a few deaths were officially recorded.
Soon men such as Christopher Wren and John Evelyn draw up plans for a new London. Pepys studies them with interest, although many owners want to rebuild their old houses as quickly as they can.
In June 1667, Dutch warships sail up the River Medway, burn several English ships and tow away the Royal Charles. Pepys is ashamed and frightened, because he knows that the Navy was not ready.

Pepys fears that the Dutch will land and march on London, so he sends his gold and papers away. His father and Elizabeth carry the family's money into the countryside, where they bury it in the garden.
In March 1668, Pepys must defend the Navy Office in front of the House of Commons. He speaks for nearly three hours, and many members praise his clear and confident speech.
Pepys's eyes begin to ache after years of reading and writing by candlelight. He buys spectacles and tries other cures, but he fears that he may soon go blind.
In October 1668, Elizabeth finds out that Pepys has been unfaithful with her young companion, Deb Willet. She is furious and heartbroken, and for weeks the household is full of tears and angry words.
On 31 May 1669, Pepys writes the last entry in his diary, because he believes he is going blind. He says that closing the book feels almost like going into his grave, and he asks God to prepare him.
Only months later, in November 1669, Elizabeth dies of a fever, aged only twenty-nine, after a journey abroad. Pepys is heartbroken, and he builds a monument to her in the church of St Olave.
Pepys never goes blind, and he continues to rise in the Navy. He becomes Secretary to the Admiralty, improves the training of officers and is chosen as President of the Royal Society.

Pepys dies in 1703 and leaves his library of about three thousand books to Magdalene College, Cambridge. The six volumes of his diary are among them, and they lie almost unread for more than a hundred years.

Today Pepys's diary is one of the most loved books in the English language. Because he wrote honestly about plague, fire, music, dinners and his own mistakes, readers feel that they are standing beside him.
C1C2: On the first day of 1660, in a small rented house in Axe Yard, Westminster, a young clerk named Samuel Pepys opened a fresh notebook and began a diary that he never expected anyone to read. He wrote it in a system of shorthand, partly to save time and partly to keep his private life from curious eyes. For nine years he would record the great events of his age beside his dinners, his quarrels and his small vanities, and the mixture is what makes the book unforgettable.

Samuel Pepys was born in London in 1633, the son of a tailor, and a good education at St Paul's School and Cambridge had lifted him a little above his family's station. At the start of 1660, however, he was only a young clerk of modest means, with a small salary, a rented house and the support of a powerful cousin. Everything about him suggested a man waiting for his chance, and that chance was just about to arrive.

In March 1658 Pepys had undergone a terrifying operation to remove a stone from his bladder, performed without anaesthetic by a surgeon who worked in a matter of minutes. Many patients died of such operations, but Pepys recovered, and he was so grateful that he kept the anniversary as a feast for the rest of his life. The diary shows him in the years that followed, a man who felt that every day was a gift.

Pepys had married Elizabeth Marchant de St Michel in 1655, when she was only fifteen years old and he was twenty-two, and she shared his small, crowded household with a servant girl and little money. Their marriage was affectionate, quarrelsome, jealous and full of laughter, and the diary notes every shade of it with startling honesty. Through Pepys's eyes we meet Elizabeth as a spirited, intelligent woman who deserved better than he sometimes gave her.

England had no king and no stable government, and in February 1660 the news that General Monck had declared for a free Parliament sent the citizens into the streets with delight. Pepys records the bonfires blazing at every corner, and he describes how the crowd roasted rumps of meat in the flames to mock the discredited Rump Parliament. It was a rough, joyful night, and it showed that the country was weary of confusion and ready for a change.

Pepys's chance came through his cousin Edward Montagu, a powerful sea commander who invited him to sail as his secretary aboard the warship Naseby. Pepys left Elizabeth, packed his few belongings and went aboard with the excitement of a boy, for the fleet was bound for Holland to bring the exiled Charles Stuart home. He wrote about every detail of ship life, from the food to the manners of the officers, and began to learn a trade that would shape the rest of his career.

Charles II stepped ashore at Dover on 25 May 1660 to the roar of cannon and the ringing of bells, and the crowds that greeted him seemed half mad with relief. Pepys had a close view of the royal family on board ship, and he noted with delight the king's friendly, easy manners. The Naseby, whose name recalled Cromwell's famous victory, was renamed the Royal Charles, as though the old order had been wiped away.

Thanks to his cousin's influence, Pepys was appointed Clerk of the Acts at the Navy Office in the summer of 1660, a post with a handsome salary and a house near the Tower of London. He had gone from uncertainty to promise in a single season, and he could hardly believe his good luck. Yet he also resolved to work hard, and through the years of the diary he keeps that promise with great energy.

The diary shows Pepys rising early to attend to the business of the Navy, checking the accounts of dockyards, questioning contractors and learning about timber, tar and rope. In 1662, at the age of twenty-nine, he humbly set out to learn the multiplication table, so that no clerk or merchant could fool him with figures. His diligence, backed by a clear and orderly mind, slowly turned a clever young man into one of the most capable officials in England.

The coronation of Charles II took place on 23 April 1661, and Pepys rose before dawn to find a place where he could see the splendid procession and the glittering ceremony in Westminster Abbey. Throughout the long day he marvelled at the colours, the music and the sheer noise of the whole occasion. That night he celebrated so enthusiastically with his friends that he went to bed drunk, and the next morning he recorded the whole business in his diary with comic regret.

Music was perhaps the greatest pleasure of Pepys's life, and the diary is full of evenings when he took up the lute, the viol or the little flageolet and played until the candles burned low. Elizabeth sang, friends joined in, and sometimes a whole company of neighbours would end the night in cheerful song. He even confessed that music was the thing in the world that he loved best, and the diary shows how much the sound of a good voice could move him.

When the theatres reopened after years of Puritan rule, Pepys became one of their most faithful customers, and his diary is a lively record of what he saw. He loved the music, the costumes and, to his shame, the actresses, but he was never afraid to give an honest opinion. After watching A Midsummer Night's Dream in 1662, he declared it the most insipid, ridiculous play that he had ever seen in his life.

Readers of the diary soon discover that Pepys was a man of healthy appetites, and he describes his meals with the relish of a true food lover: oysters, pies, roast beef and fine wines. Nothing pleased him more than a successful dinner party, when the table was full, the conversation lively and the wine well chosen. Behind such details lies a precious record of how people ate in the seventeenth century, from the humblest breakfast to the grandest feast.

Coffee was a fashionable novelty in London, and Pepys became a regular visitor to the coffee-houses, where merchants, sailors, scholars and politicians gathered to share news and argue about it. He listened eagerly, for gossip was the raw material of power, and a clerk who knew what was being said could often guess what would be done. Such places helped to make London a city of conversation, and Pepys seems to have been happiest when he was in the middle of it.

Fashion mattered to Pepys, and in 1663 he took the great step of buying a periwig, the long curled wig that a gentleman of the day was expected to wear. He hesitated for weeks over the cost and over what his neighbours would say, and when he finally appeared in public with it he felt both proud and slightly foolish. Like everything else, this small adventure went into his diary, and now it tells us how people felt about their looks more than three hundred years ago.

Part of the charm of the diary is that Pepys never pretends to be perfect, and he repeatedly made solemn vows to give up wine, theatres and wasteful pleasures. He kept them for a few weeks, sometimes for months, and then some temptation would arrive and the vow was quietly broken. Few diarists have been so frank about their weaknesses, and that frankness gives us the feeling of knowing him.

Elizabeth began to learn dancing from a master named Mr Pembleton, and Pepys, who had paid for the lessons, found himself consumed by jealousy whenever the two took hands. He watched the pair, brooded for days and let the little affair spoil his temper and his sleep. In the end nothing more than dancing was proved, but the episode shows how a man who ruled a naval office could be ruled by his own heart.

In December 1664 a brilliant comet streaked across the winter sky, and Pepys, like half of London, stood in the cold to watch it with a mixture of wonder and unease. Some of his neighbours were sure that it announced a disaster, and Pepys, though more sceptical, did not feel able to laugh at them. He did not yet know that within months the plague would reach London, and that many would say the comet had foretold it.

In January 1665 Pepys bought Robert Hooke's Micrographia, a book of drawings made with the microscope, and he sat up until two in the morning, calling it the most ingenious book he had ever read. The pictures of fleas, lice and the point of a needle astonished him, and they opened his mind to a new world of science. Only weeks later he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society, the learned club that was changing how Englishmen thought about nature.

The Second Dutch War broke out in 1665, and the burden of finding food, sails, powder and men for the fleet fell upon the Navy Office, where Pepys laboured from dawn until dark. In June the English fleet won a bloody victory off Lowestoft, and the whole city rejoiced at the news. Pepys shared in the rejoicing, but he also knew how close the thing had been, and how thin the money was that paid for it.

On 7 June 1665, walking through Drury Lane, Pepys saw for himself the red cross that marked a plague house, with the words Lord have mercy upon us written on the door beside it. He wrote that he had never seen houses shut up in his life, and that the sight made him feel so unwell that he bought some roll tobacco to smell and chew. It was a small purchase, but the diary shows how quickly fear could enter an ordinary mind.

With the death toll mounting, Pepys made his will and put his accounts in order, and he sent Elizabeth and most of the household out of London to the safety of a town down the river. He himself stayed at his post, partly out of duty and partly because the war did not stop for a plague. The diary at this time is strangely cheerful and strangely afraid, and he often seems surprised by his own courage.

As the summer wore on, Pepys walked through a city that no longer seemed like London, with shut shops, silent streets and grass growing in the courtyards of Whitehall. The tolling of funeral bells was constant, and he noticed that people gave one another a wide berth in the street and looked at passers-by with open suspicion. He wrote it all down without exaggeration, and his plain, steady sentences strike harder than any more elaborate description could.

Pepys lost friends, neighbours and colleagues to the plague, and the diary records their names one after another with a quiet, helpless sorrow. He was ashamed of his own fear, yet he never shrank from his work, and he moved between London and the dockyards in order to keep the fleet supplied. Duty gave him something to hold on to in the darkest weeks, and it may have saved his sanity as much as his life.

In September 1665 the weekly bill reached a total of more than seven thousand burials, the worst figures yet seen, and Pepys studied it with a sinking heart. He feared, as many others did, that the real figure was nearer ten thousand, since the poorest victims and those buried in haste were never fully counted. The numbers were almost too large to imagine, and he went on with his work, because there was nothing else to do.

As winter set in, the bills fell steadily, and Pepys noticed more people in the streets and more shops open for business. He confessed in the diary that, despite the horrors around him, he had never lived so merrily as during the plague time, partly because he was earning so well. It is a rare and honest confession, and it reminds us that great disasters are lived by people with mixed feelings.

In June 1666 the thunder of guns from the Four Days' Battle was heard in the south-east of England, and Pepys, like everyone else in the Navy Office, waited anxiously for news. When the reports came, they told of a bloody and confused struggle in which the English fleet lost several ships and many men. The war had turned grim, and Pepys's task of finding money, stores and sailors seemed heavier with every post.

The King's money was always short, and the sailors who risked their lives for the fleet were sometimes paid late or not at all, while dockyard workers also waited for their wages. Pepys, who had to face the angry men at his door, found himself caught between their needs and the empty treasury. His letters and diary entries from this period show a conscientious official who knew that a navy without pay is a navy on the edge of collapse.

At three o'clock in the morning on Sunday, 2 September 1666, Pepys's maid Jane woke him with news of a large fire in the City, and he went to the window in his nightgown. He judged that it was a good way off and not likely to reach his own house, and so, with an easy mind, he went back to bed and slept. It is a haunting moment, because we know what he did not, that this ordinary Sunday was the beginning of one of the greatest disasters in the city's history.

When he rose again, Pepys heard that more than three hundred houses had already burned in the night, and he hurried to the Tower of London and climbed to a high place for a view. There he saw the houses at the end of London Bridge in flames, and a vast fire raging on both sides, driven by a strong wind from the east. The sight sobered him at once, and he understood that this was no ordinary fire but a catastrophe that could swallow the whole city.

Pepys took a boat on the river to see the fire for himself, and he saw the water crowded with barges and small craft, piled high with furniture and bedding and whatever families could grab. Along the banks the people were hurrying to save what they could, and he noticed that even the pigeons were reluctant to leave their homes, circling the burning windows until their wings caught fire and they fell. The little detail, so tender in the midst of ruin, is one of the most famous in the whole diary.

Pepys took boat to Whitehall and was brought before King Charles II and the Duke of York, to whom he described how swiftly the fire was spreading and how little was done to stop it. The King, deeply concerned, ordered Pepys to carry a message to the Lord Mayor, commanding him to pull down houses in the fire's path before the flames could reach them. It was a moment when a clerk of the Navy became, for a few hours, a messenger of the nation's fate.

In Cannon Street, Pepys found the Lord Mayor, Sir Thomas Bloodworth, worn out and nearly in tears, crying that he was spent and that the people would not obey him. The fire, he said, was overtaking the houses faster than his workmen could pull them down, and Pepys left him with a heavy heart and little confidence in the city's rulers. In that single scene the diary captures the helplessness of authority in the face of an unstoppable disaster.

As darkness fell, Pepys and some friends took a boat to the south bank of the river and sat in an alehouse, watching the flames climb into the night sky. The fire, he wrote, formed one great arch of light across the water, a horrid, malicious, bloody flame that was nothing like the gentle blaze of a hearth. They stayed until the heat and the falling sparks drove them away, and Pepys went home to a troubled night.

On Monday the fire still raged, and Pepys spent the day moving his money, his best goods and his papers to places of safety, while carts could be had only at ruinous prices. At one point he paid a huge sum for a single cart, and the narrow streets were so crowded with refugees that every journey took hours. Around him the old city was melting away, and every family was deciding what could be saved and what must be lost.

On the night of 4 September, with the flames drawing nearer, Pepys and his neighbour Sir William Penn dug a pit in the garden and buried their best wine and a precious Parmesan cheese. It is perhaps the best-loved moment in the diary, a scene of two serious officials with spades trying to save their dinner from a burning city. Behind the comedy, of course, lies real fear, for men do not bury their cheese unless they believe the worst.

Sir William Penn, thinking quickly, brought workmen from the dockyards at Deptford to pull down houses around the Navy Office, and this firebreak, together with a change in the wind, saved the building. The flames reached the neighbouring church of All Hallows, Barking, and then, to the astonishment of the exhausted crowd, they stopped. Pepys, who had spent four days in terror, found that his home and his office had been spared, though the greater part of the city around him lay in ashes.

When the flames at last died away, Pepys walked through the burnt streets on foot, picking his way over heaps of rubble and past walls that still smoked. The ground was so hot that it almost burned the soles of his shoes, and he saw no familiar landmarks in what had been the busiest streets in England. It was a ghostly landscape, and he described it with a clerk's eye for detail and a human being's shock.

By the time it was over, the Great Fire had destroyed about thirteen thousand houses and eighty-seven churches, including the old Cathedral of St Paul, and tens of thousands of Londoners were left without shelter. Remarkably, only a handful of deaths were officially recorded, although historians suspect that the true number may have been higher. The loss was immense, yet the fire also cleared the ground for a new and better city, and Pepys lived to see the beginning of it.

Within days, men such as Christopher Wren and John Evelyn were drawing up plans for a rebuilt London with broad, straight streets, and Pepys followed the debate eagerly. In the end most of the grand plans were set aside, because property owners wanted to rebuild on their old plots as quickly as they could. Even so, the new city was built of brick and stone, with somewhat wider streets, and it was safer than the one the fire had destroyed.

In June 1667 a Dutch fleet sailed boldly up the River Medway, set fire to several English warships and towed away the Royal Charles, the very ship that had brought Charles II home seven years before. The humiliation was deep, for the great navy that Englishmen had boasted of had been outmatched in its own waters while its men waited unpaid. Pepys, who had long warned that the money would run out, felt both deep shame and a bitter sense of having been proved right.

In the panic that followed, many Londoners believed that the Dutch might march on the capital, and Pepys prepared for the worst by sending his gold and his key papers out of the city. His father and Elizabeth travelled to the countryside carrying the family's money, which they buried in a garden at night, and the whole scheme seems to have been conducted in a fever of secrecy. When the danger passed, the gold had to be dug up again, and the diary tells with some humour how hard it was to find it all.

In the spring of 1668, a Parliamentary inquiry into the failures of the war put the Navy Office on trial, and Pepys rose before the House of Commons to defend it. He spoke for nearly three hours, calmly and from the notes he had prepared, and when he sat down many members congratulated him with real warmth. For a man who had grown up as a tailor's son, it was a day of glory, and he recorded every compliment in his diary with simple, unashamed joy.

Years of reading and writing by weak candlelight were taking their toll, and from 1668 the diary is full of complaints about Pepys's failing eyes. He bought spectacles, tried various cures, and even had a special shade made to keep the glare from his face, but nothing seemed to help. The prospect of blindness filled him with dread, for the diary was one of the greatest pleasures of his life.

One of the most painful episodes in the diary comes in October 1668, when Elizabeth caught her husband in an embrace with Deb Willet, a young woman who lived in the house as her companion. The household was thrown into turmoil, and Pepys, ashamed and afraid of losing his wife, wrote of his own guilt and her anger with a candour that few men would dare. In time the couple were reconciled, but the diary suggests that the trust between them had been seriously damaged.

On 31 May 1669, after nine years and about one and a quarter million words, Pepys wrote the final entry of his diary, convinced that his failing eyes would soon leave him unable to see. He said that giving up the diary seemed almost like seeing himself go into his grave, and he prayed that God would prepare him for the discomforts of blindness. The words are simple and moving, and the man who wrote them could not know that he would still be reading and writing decades later.

Only a few months after the diary ended, in November 1669, Elizabeth died of a fever at the age of twenty-nine, soon after returning with Pepys from a journey to France and the Netherlands. He was heartbroken, and he commissioned a marble monument to her in the church of St Olave, Hart Street, where it can still be seen today. He never married again, and when he died more than thirty years later he was laid to rest beside her in the same church.

To everyone's surprise, including his own, Pepys's eyesight did not fail, and the hard-working official went on to a long and distinguished career. As Secretary to the Admiralty he improved the training of naval officers, introduced examinations for lieutenants and fought corruption, so that the English fleet grew stronger and better managed. He was also elected President of the Royal Society in 1684, and Newton's Principia appeared with his approval printed on the title page.

Pepys died in 1703 and left his library of about three thousand books to Magdalene College, Cambridge, and the six leather volumes of his shorthand diary lay quietly among them. For well over a century almost nobody read them, until a student named John Smith patiently deciphered the shorthand, and a selection was published in 1825 to great astonishment. A complete edition, with the passages once thought too frank to print, did not appear until the 1970s and 1980s.

More than three centuries later, Pepys's diary is still read for pleasure by people all over the world, because it makes the seventeenth century feel as close as yesterday. He never meant to be a writer, yet his honesty, curiosity and humour gave us the finest portrait we have of London under Charles II. What he left, in the end, is the sound of a real man's voice speaking quietly across the years, and it is still worth listening to.
